segments.say: Almost every home has one. A high cupboard, a special tin, a drawer that's only opened on Sundays. Inside, the treats that children are not supposed to have, or at least not yet. It's one of the most natural rules a loving parent can make. And it's one of the most interesting places to watch reactance at work.

Picture a small child who knows exactly where the biscuits are kept. Every visit to the kitchen comes with a glance at that cupboard. Can I have one? Just one? Please? The treat is barely visible, and yet it seems to occupy half the child's thoughts.

So here's what researchers wanted to know. When we put a tasty food out of reach, does that help children eat less of it? Or does the rule itself make the food more desirable, so that they want it more, and eat more of it the moment they get the chance?

show.sub: Does keeping it away make it matter more?

segments.say: In a study published in 1999, Jennifer Fisher and Leann Birch worked with preschool children, aged around three to five. Over several weeks, the children were offered two similar, tasty snacks. One was freely available. The other was placed in a clear jar, where the children could see it, but could only have it during short, limited moments.

show.what: Restricting access to palatable foods affects children's behavioral response, food selection, and intake

segments.say: The restricted snack quickly became the star of the show. When the jar was opened, the children paid more attention to it, asked for it more, reached for it more, and ate more of it than they had before the restriction began. The snack itself hadn't changed at all. Only its status had. And remember, the two snacks had been chosen to be very similar. The only real difference between them was the rule. One was simply there. The other was something you had to wait for.

If this sounds familiar, it should. It's the same pattern we met with scarce cookies and banned products. Something that is hard to get feels more precious. And for a small child, a clear jar that is only opened now and then is about as precious as it gets.

There's something clever about the clear jar in that study. The children could see the snack all the time, but they couldn't decide when to have it. That's a very particular kind of feeling. The food was always present, and always just out of their control. It's hard to imagine a better recipe for wanting something more.

Notice that none of these were what the rule intended. The aim of restriction is usually to reduce how much of a food a child eats. In the short run, at the moments when the food did appear, it seemed to do the opposite.

show.title: What restriction did to the snack
items: More eating when it was allowed

segments.say: A few years later, a team in the Netherlands made the experiment even simpler. No jars, no weeks of restriction. Just one small rule, given once.

show.title: Do not eat the red ones

segments.say: In 2007, Anita Jansen and her colleagues gave children a bowl of small sweets in several colours. Some of the children were told not to eat the red ones. Other children were given no rule at all. Later, all the children were allowed to eat whichever sweets they liked.

show.who: Anita Jansen, Sandra Mulkens & Arnoud Jansen
show.what: Do not eat the red food! Prohibition of snacks leads to their relatively higher consumption in children

segments.say: Once the rule was lifted, the children who had been told not to eat the red sweets ate relatively more of the red ones than the children who had never heard any rule. The colour itself made no difference to the taste. What changed was that red had become the forbidden colour, and forbidden things seem to taste a little sweeter.

This is where reactance and the white bear meet. A rule like don't eat the red ones does two things at once. It threatens a small freedom, which invites pushback. And it keeps the forbidden food at the front of the mind, which makes it harder to forget. Both point in the same direction.

show.sub: A rule that keeps the food in mind

segments.say: And the effect doesn't always stay at the table. A child who learns that a certain food is special and forbidden may carry that feeling for years. The cupboard becomes a little shrine. The treat becomes a reward, a comfort, a prize. Ordinary food can slowly turn into something much more loaded than it ever needed to be.

show.sub: A rule can outlast the moment

segments.say: None of this means children should be given unlimited sweets. That's not what the researchers suggested. But it does mean that how a food is handled can change the way children feel about it, sometimes for longer than we'd expect.
And it works the other way round, too. If forbidding a food can make it more tempting, what happens when we push children towards a food instead? Finish your vegetables, and then you can play.

show.cap: When healthy food becomes a chore
show.sub: The other side of the rule

segments.say: In 1984, Leann Birch and her colleagues gave preschool children a drink they hadn't tasted before. For some children, drinking it was the condition for getting to do something fun afterwards. Other children simply had the drink, with no deal attached. Then the researchers measured how much the children liked the drink, and compared the two groups.

show.who: Leann Birch, Diane Marlin & Julie Rotter
show.what: Eating as the means activity in a contingency: effects on young children's food preference

segments.say: The children who had been asked to drink it in order to earn a reward ended up liking it less. The deal had sent a quiet message. This is something you have to get through to reach the good part. And children, like the rest of us, are very good at reading between the lines.

show.sub: The deal made it less liked

segments.say: It's worth saying that these were small studies with young children, in particular settings. They don't mean that every rule about food will backfire, or that every reward ruins a vegetable forever. But together, they point to a pattern that many parents will recognise from their own kitchen.

The idea isn't to give up on guidance. It's to take the drama out of it. A treat that is simply part of life, now and then, tends to lose some of its magic. And a vegetable that isn't a hurdle has a better chance of becoming a friend.

show.title: Gentler ways to handle treats
items: Offer them now and then, calmly, with no big fuss
Serve healthy foods often, without deals or bribes
Eat well together and let children copy you

segments.say: And if you're smiling at all this, thinking of your own childhood, it's worth noticing that adults do it too. A strict diet that bans a favourite food can make that food feel more tempting than ever. The jar may be different. The feeling is much the same. Often, the healthiest relationship with food is one where nothing is completely off-limits, and nothing is a battle.

But here's something you may have noticed along the way. Not every child grabs for the jar, and not every adult rebels against a rule. Some people seem to shrug off a ban, while others feel it like a pebble in their shoe. So who reacts most strongly, and why? That's what we'll explore next.

show.sub: Some of us push back harder
